subtopics.title: From First Villages to an Urban World

questions.question: The recipe that made the first towns possible was:
options: Farming surplus plus specialisation plus exchange
Gold plus railways plus harbours
Factories plus electricity plus roads
Armies plus taxes plus walls

questions.question: The first true urban settlements appeared in:
options: Mountain fortresses of central Asia
Irrigated river valleys such as the Nile, Tigris-Euphrates and Indus
Coastal fishing villages of the Pacific
Desert oases of the Sahara

questions.question: Comparing the developed and developing worlds today:
options: Both have identical levels and rates of urbanisation
Developed countries have low levels and fast rates
Developed countries have high levels but slow rates; developing countries have lower levels but rapid rates
Developing countries have stopped urbanising entirely

questions.question: Urbanisation differs from urban growth in that urbanisation is:
options: The increase in the PERCENTAGE of the population that is urban, while urban growth is the increase in the NUMBER of urban residents
The building of new towns, while urban growth is their maintenance
Movement into cities, while urban growth is movement out
A rural process, while urban growth is coastal

questions.question: Rate of urbanisation versus level of urbanisation is best summarised as:
options: Number against percentage
Speed of the climb against the snapshot percentage at a moment
Cities against towns
Expansion against sprawl

questions.question: Urban sprawl differs from urban expansion because sprawl is:
options: Any growth of the built-up area
Growth limited to the CBD
Vertical growth through high-rise building
Low-density, unplanned or poorly planned outward spread — estates leapfrogging along highways, farmland consumed

questions.question: Counter-urbanisation describes:
options: Rural workers commuting into cities daily
The densification of inner-city housing
People moving out of large cities to small towns and rural areas, as with remote workers settling in Garden Route towns
Governments blocking migration to cities

subtopics.title: Site, Situation and the Functional Classification of Towns

questions.question: Johannesburg proves that a town can succeed with:
options: A poor site, when its situation — astride the Witwatersrand gold — is valuable enough
No site at all
A perfect site and no situation
Neither site nor situation

questions.question: A central place is defined as a settlement whose main function is to:
options: Transfer cargo between transport modes
Provide goods and services to its surrounding region — its sphere of influence
Guard a mountain pass
House factory workers

questions.question: Richards Bay, where coal moves from trains into bulk carriers, is the example of a:
options: Gap town
Central place
Break-of-bulk point, where industry gathers to process cargo that must be handled anyway
Resort town

questions.question: Correct pairings of specialised towns and functions include:
options: Welkom — tourism; Hermanus — mining
Secunda — education; Stellenbosch — fuel-from-coal
Bhisho — mining; Welkom — administration
Welkom — mining; Secunda — fuel-from-coal; Stellenbosch — education; Bhisho — administration

subtopics.title: Urban Hierarchy and Land-Use Zones: The Anatomy of a City

questions.question: The see-saw rule of the urban hierarchy states that:
options: There are many small places offering low-order services and few large places offering high-order ones
All towns offer the same services
Large cities outnumber small towns
High-order services are found in every village

questions.question: The CBD's signature trio is:
options: Cheapest land, oldest houses, quietest streets
Highest land values, tallest buildings, greatest accessibility
Most factories, widest roads, biggest gardens
Lowest rents, most residents, least transport

questions.question: The transition zone around the CBD is characterised by:
options: Uniform high-income housing
Untouched natural vegetation
Mixed, changing land use — subdivided old houses, light industry, decay and gentrification side by side
Heavy industry and container terminals

questions.question: Apartheid planning deformed the residential gradient by:
options: Building all housing at equal distance from work
Moving factories into the suburbs
Placing high-income suburbs beside the harbours
Siting townships like Mdantsane and Mamelodi on the far urban edge, behind buffer strips and industrial belts, far from work

subtopics.title: Why Cities Exist and Why Everyone Is Moving to Them

questions.question: The 'surplus secret' of the first towns is that extra food:
options: Freed some people from farming to specialise and trade at one gathering spot
Was burned to clear land for building
Attracted wild animals that people hunted
Was exported to other continents

questions.question: Factories accelerated urbanisation because a factory:
options: Requires farmland to operate
Is a gathering machine, pulling thousands of workers to a single gate
Can only be built in villages
Reduces the need for workers

questions.question: In the parked-car picture, the car still accelerating up the slope represents:
options: Developed countries with high levels and slow rates
Countries that are fully rural
Developing countries — urban level still climbing at a high rate
Cities that have stopped growing

subtopics.title: The Ladder of Shops and the Jobs Towns Do

questions.question: The shopping-trip rule of the hierarchy says that:
options: Everything is bought in the largest city
The more ordinary the purchase, the nearer and more numerous the places selling it; the more special, the further and fewer
Special goods are sold at every spaza
Distance has no relation to what is sold

questions.question: A gap town such as Ceres or Tulbagh exists because it:
options: Sits at a natural passage through a mountain barrier and collects the funnelled traffic
Owns the largest dam in the region
Was built beside a gold reef
Controls an international border

questions.question: Komatipoort is classified as a gateway town because it:
options: Serves surrounding farms with groceries
Processes coal into fuel
Holds the door where routes cross the Mozambique border
Hosts a university

questions.question: 'Towns forgive a bad site for a good enough reason' is proven by:
options: Cape Town, which has no harbour
Hermanus, which has no tourists
Ceres, which has no mountains
Johannesburg — a poor site overruled by a situation on the richest gold ever found

subtopics.title: A Taxi Ride Across the Zones

questions.question: The CBD's towers exist because of a tug-of-war in which:
options: Every business wants the most accessible ground, so land costs a fortune and floors are stacked to pay for it
Builders compete to use the most concrete
The city requires all offices to be tall
Tall buildings avoid property tax

questions.question: The 'half construction site, half waiting room' ring of subdivided houses and renovations is the:
options: Industrial belt
Transition zone
Decentralised node
High-income suburb

questions.question: Heavy industry stretches along railways and highways because it:
options: Wants views of the mountains
Must stay inside the CBD
Needs flat ground and bulk transport, at a distance from high-value housing
Employs no workers

questions.question: Decentralised nodes like Menlyn, uMhlanga Ridge and Canal Walk have the effect of:
options: Increasing CBD land values everywhere
Ending suburban shopping entirely
Moving all factories into the city centre
Pulling CBD functions out to the highways and suburbs, leaving some old downtowns to decline and pursue renewal
